Hurling offers a good range of betting markets, from simple match bets to season-long outrights. Here are the ones you'll come across most often.

Match Winner. The most straightforward hurling bet — you're backing one team to win a single game. In the provincial round-robins, a draw is possible, so many match-winner markets are priced as three outcomes (home win, away win or draw); in knockout games the tie will be settled on the day.

Handicap / Points Start. Because hurling scorelines can be lopsided, bookmakers apply a handicap to level the market. The favourite is given a points deficit to overcome and the underdog a head start, which often gives a more appealing price than backing a strong favourite outright.

Total Points (Over/Under). Here you're betting on the combined points scored by both teams, rather than who wins. Hurling is a high-scoring sport, so these lines are set high — a useful market when you fancy an open, attacking game or a tighter defensive battle.

Outright Winner. These are the season-long, ante-post markets — betting on who will lift the Liam MacCarthy Cup, or the Mick Mackey and Bob O'Keeffe Cups in Munster and Leinster. Prices are longest before a ball is thrown in and shorten as the Championship unfolds, so early value is often found here.

Top Scorer & First Goalscorer. Popular for bigger games, these markets let you back individual players — either to score the game's first goal or to finish as a match or Championship top scorer. Free-taking specialists tend to dominate the scoring charts, which is worth factoring in.

Whichever market you're weighing up, our tipsters' hurling picks above cover a broad spread of them, each with the reasoning behind the selection.

Road to the All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship

The All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship was established in 1887 and crowns the best hurling team in Ireland. Teams reach the All-Ireland series through the Leinster and Munster Championships, and where they finish in their provincial group decides how far into the knockout stages they enter.

In both the Leinster and Munster Championships, the group winners advance straight to the All-Ireland semi-finals, the runners-up move into the quarter-finals, and the third-placed teams also progress to the quarter-finals. The quarter-final ties pair each province's runners-up against the other province's third-placed side — so the Munster runners-up face Leinster's third-placed team, and the Leinster runners-up face Munster's third-placed team.

From 2026, the preliminary quarter-finals were scrapped, meaning the Joe McDonagh Cup finalists no longer feed into the All-Ireland series at this stage. The upshot for bettors is simple: the stronger a county's provincial campaign, the fewer knockout games it needs to win to lift the Liam MacCarthy Cup.

The Munster Senior Hurling Championship

The Munster Senior Hurling Championship is contested for the Mick Mackey Cup and is widely regarded as the toughest provincial competition in the sport. Five counties — traditionally Cork, Clare, Limerick, Tipperary and Waterford — meet in a round-robin group, each playing the other once, with two points for a win and one for a draw.

The top two advance to the Munster final, where the champions progress to the All-Ireland semi-finals and the runners-up to the quarter-finals. The third-placed county also reaches the All-Ireland quarter-finals. A promotion and relegation system normally links the bottom of the Munster group with the Joe McDonagh Cup, hurling's second tier, though the counties involved vary from season to season. With so little between the leading counties, Munster fixtures are among the most competitive — and most heavily bet — of the hurling calendar. Limerick have dominated the province in recent years, though Cork and Clare have shown they can go toe-to-toe with the best.

The Leinster Senior Hurling Championship

The Leinster Senior Hurling Championship is played for the Bob O'Keeffe Cup and follows the same format as its Munster counterpart, with six counties competing in a round-robin group. Kilkenny and Galway are the traditional heavyweights, joined in recent seasons by the likes of Dublin, Wexford and Offaly.

As in Munster, the top two teams contest the provincial final, with the champions advancing to the All-Ireland semi-finals and the runners-up to the quarter-finals. The third-placed county joins them in the All-Ireland quarter-finals, while the lowest-placed side is relegated to the Joe McDonagh Cup, with the McDonagh Cup winner promoted in its place. Kilkenny have historically been the dominant force in Leinster hurling, holding by far the most provincial titles, which makes them a familiar name near the top of the outright betting each season.
All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship Past Winners

Below are the last ten winners of the All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship. The final has been played at Croke Park in Dublin since 1914, with the sole exception of 1937, when it was staged at FitzGerald Stadium, Killarney.

Kilkenny are the most successful county with 36 titles, though the last of those came back in 2015. Cork sit second on 30, while Tipperary moved to 29 with their 2025 triumph. Limerick, meanwhile, have been the dominant force of the modern era, and their 2026 win over Galway took them to 13 titles — including six of the last nine championships.

FAQ

Hurling Betting Tips FAQs

  • Limerick won the 2026 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship, beating Galway 1-29 to 1-18 in the final at Croke Park on 19 July 2026. It was Limerick's 13th title and their first since 2023.

  • Kilkenny are the most successful county in All-Ireland hurling history with 36 titles, ahead of Cork on 30 and Tipperary on 29. Kilkenny's most recent title came in 2015.

  • The inter-county hurling Championship runs from spring to summer, with the provincial round-robins beginning in April, the Munster and Leinster finals in early June, and the All-Ireland final held at Croke Park in July.

  • The most popular hurling betting markets are match winner, handicap (or points start), total points, and outright winner markets for the provincial championships and the All-Ireland. Many bookmakers also price up first goalscorer and top team scorer markets for big games.

  • Hurling is an outdoor stick-and-ball team sport of ancient Gaelic and Irish origin, played with a wooden stick called a hurley and a small ball known as a sliotar. It's one of Ireland's two main Gaelic games alongside Gaelic Football and is governed by the GAA.

  • OLBG's hurling tips are posted by community tipsters, each with a visible strike rate and profit history so you can follow the most reliable form. Every tip shows the selection, the odds, a confidence rating and the number of tips placed, helping you judge which picks carry the most support.
